§0Orientation · LO1

The pectoral girdle — a limb hung for movement

One strut, one blade, and a shallow socket: built for reach, not for safety.

The pectoral girdle is an incomplete bony ring of two bones — the clavicle and scapula — that slings the whole upper limb onto the trunk (Plate 0.1). It links the free limb to the back (via posterior thoracoappendicular muscles) and to the anterior thorax (via the manubrium of the sternum).

  • The clavicle is a rigid strut that props the scapula and limb away from the thorax — creating room for maximal swing.
  • The scapula glides freely on the chest wall at the conceptual scapulothoracic "joint" (not a true joint — no cartilage/capsule, just muscle-slung bone on ribs).
Label Key — Pectoral girdle (superior view)
Clavicle
The anterior strut; its only bony link to the axial skeleton is medially, at the sternum.
Scapula
The posterior blade; held to the chest wall by muscle, free to slide and rotate.
Rib I / thoracic inlet
The girdle sits atop the first rib; the axillary inlet is the gateway of vessels/nerves to the limb.
Manubrium (sternal link)
The single skeletal attachment of the whole girdle to the trunk — at the sternoclavicular joint.
Reasoning · why learn the bones before the joints and muscles

Every joint, ligament and muscle in this lecture is named after a bony landmark — the supraglenoid tubercle, the coracoid process, the greater tubercle, the intertubercular groove. Learn the bony map first (§1) and the joints (§2) and muscles (§3) become a story of what attaches where and why. So we do the clavicle, scapula and humerus first — then hang everything else on them.

Reasoning · the shoulder's founding trade-off — mobility vs stability

The upper limb's job is to place the hand anywhere, so evolution maximised range of motion at the cost of bony security. The girdle attaches to the trunk at only one small joint (sternoclavicular), the scapula floats on muscle, and the ball sits in a shallow, oversized-ball socket. The payoff is huge reach; the price is instability — which is why dislocation, rotator-cuff problems and muscle-dependent stability dominate the clinical picture (§2–3).

R Recall checklist — orientation
  • Pectoral girdle = clavicle + scapula (an incomplete ring); its only axial link is the sternoclavicular joint.
  • Clavicle = rigid strut holding the limb off the thorax; scapula = free blade on the scapulothoracic surface.
  • Design theme: maximal mobility, minimal bony stability — the source of most shoulder pathology.
  • Learn order: bones → joints → muscles (everything is named off a bony landmark).
§1Bones · LO1-2

Bones of the shoulder region

Clavicle, scapula and proximal humerus — every landmark earns its keep.

§1.1Clavicle

  • Shape: a long bone with a double curve — from above it looks like an elongated "S". The medial 2/3 of the body is convex forward; the lateral 1/3 is concave forward.
  • Sternal (medial) end — enlarged and triangular; articulates with the sternum at the sternoclavicular joint.
  • Acromial (lateral) end — flat; articulates with the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint.
  • Superior surface — smooth (lies just under the skin). Inferior surface — rough, from strong attachments.

Inferior-surface attachments (the roughness): (a) the two bands of the coracoclavicular ligament — the trapezoid line and conoid tubercle; (b) the costoclavicular ligament (medially, to rib 1); (c) the subclavius muscle in the subclavian groove.

Label Key — Clavicle
Sternal end (medial)
Enlarged, triangular; the sternoclavicular joint — the limb's only bony link to the trunk.
Acromial end (lateral)
Flat; the acromioclavicular joint with the scapula.
Superior surface
Smooth and subcutaneous — you can palpate the whole bone.
Conoid tubercle / trapezoid line
Inferior roughenings for the two bands of the coracoclavicular ligament (§2.2).
Subclavian groove
Houses subclavius; the costoclavicular ligament anchors medially to rib 1.
Reasoning · why the S-curve matters and where it snaps

The double curve lets the clavicle act as a spring/strut that transmits impact from the upper limb to the axial skeleton while allowing the scapula to swing. But the curves also create a mechanical weak point: the junction of the middle and lateral thirds (where convex meets concave) is where force concentrates.

Clinical · the clavicle is the most commonly fractured long bone

A fall on the shoulder or an outstretched hand drives force along the strut; it fails at the middle/lateral-third junction. Typically the medial fragment is pulled up by sternocleidomastoid and the lateral fragment drops (weight of the limb + pull of pectoralis/deltoid). It is so exposed and load-bearing that fractures are common — yet the very strong sternoclavicular joint rarely dislocates (§2.1).

§1.2Scapula

A flat, triangular bone. Learn it as 2 surfaces · 2 angles · 3 borders · 3 processes:

  • 2 surfaces — costal (anterior, facing ribs) and posterior.
  • 2 angles — superior and inferior.
  • 3 borders — lateral, medial and superior.
  • 3 processes — coracoid, acromion and the spine of the scapula.
Label Key — Scapula (overview)
Glenoid cavity
Shallow socket on the enlarged superolateral border for the humeral head — deepened by the glenoid labrum.
Coracoid process
Hook-like anterior process; attachment for pec minor, coracobrachialis, short head of biceps + coracoclavicular/coracoacromial ligaments.
Acromion
Lateral shelf of the spine; roofs the joint and meets the clavicle (AC joint).
Spine of the scapula
Divides the posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.
Medial & lateral borders
Muscle attachments (rhomboids/serratus medially; teres muscles laterally).

The socket and its tenants (Plate 1.3):

  • Glenoid cavity — shallow articular surface; the fibrocartilage glenoid labrum deepens it for the humeral head.
  • Supraglenoid tubercle (above glenoid) — origin of the long head of biceps.
  • Infraglenoid tubercle (below glenoid) — origin of the long head of triceps.
  • Fossae — supraspinous (→ supraspinatus), infraspinous (→ infraspinatus), and the costal subscapular fossa (→ subscapularis).
Label Key — Scapula (attachments)
Supraglenoid tubercle
Origin of the long head of biceps brachii (its tendon runs up over the humeral head).
Infraglenoid tubercle
Origin of the long head of triceps brachii.
Supraspinous fossa
Above the spine — houses supraspinatus (a rotator-cuff muscle).
Infraspinous fossa
Below the spine — houses infraspinatus (a rotator-cuff muscle).
Subscapular fossa
Shallow concavity on the costal surface — fills with subscapularis.
Memory hook · reading the scapula

2-2-3-3 = 2 surfaces, 2 angles, 3 borders, 3 processes. And the tubercles pair with the long heads: supraglenoid → biceps (up top), infraglenoid → triceps (below).

Reasoning · why the glenoid is shallow and needs a labrum

A deep socket would grip the humeral head like a hip and kill range of motion. Instead the glenoid is shallow and small (it takes only a third of the head), trading grip for a huge arc of movement. The labrum deepens it ~50% and the rotator cuff (§3.5) actively holds the head in — so stability is soft-tissue-dependent, not bony. Tear the labrum (a Bankart lesion) and the joint dislocates more easily.

§1.3Proximal humerus

The proximal end of the arm bone carries the ball plus a cluster of muscle landmarks (Plate 1.4):

  • Head — the ball; faces medially, superiorly and posteriorly into the glenoid.
  • Anatomical neck — the old growth-plate line, just below the articular head.
  • Greater & lesser tubercles — lateral and anterior bumps; rotator-cuff insertion sites.
  • Intertubercular (bicipital) groove — between the tubercles; holds the long head of biceps tendon. Its medial lip, floor and lateral lip are the three attachment sites of the "lady between two majors".
  • Surgical neck — the constriction below the tubercles; the common fracture site (and where the axillary nerve wraps).
  • Deltoid tuberosity — mid-shaft, lateral; insertion of deltoid.
Label Key — Proximal humerus
Head + anatomical neck
The articular ball and the line just distal to it (the fused growth plate).
Greater tubercle
Lateral; insertion of supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor (3 of the 4 cuff muscles).
Lesser tubercle
Anterior; insertion of subscapularis (the 4th cuff muscle).
Intertubercular (bicipital) groove
Guides the long head of biceps; lips + floor = 'lady between two majors' (§3).
Surgical neck
Common fracture site; the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex vessels wind around it.
Deltoid tuberosity
Mid-shaft insertion of deltoid.
Clinical · surgical neck fracture and the axillary nerve

The surgical neck is the weak point below the tubercles, and the axillary nerve curls right around it (with the posterior circumflex humeral artery). A surgical-neck fracture (or an anterior-inferior dislocation, §2.3) can injure the axillary nerve → deltoid paralysis (loss of abduction) and a patch of numbness over the 'regimental badge' area of the lateral shoulder.

Memory hook · the three lips of the bicipital groove

Lady between two majors: Latissimus dorsi in the floor, with Pectoralis major on the lateral lip and Teres major on the medial lip. (A lady — Latissimus — flanked by two 'majors'.)

§1.4Bones on medical imaging

The same landmarks appear on radiographs — recognise the clavicle's S, the scapular spine/acromion, the glenoid, and the humeral head/tubercles/surgical neck (Plate 1.5). This is how fractures and dislocations are read.

Label Key — Shoulder radiographs
Clavicle & acromion
Trace the strut to the AC joint; a widened AC gap suggests separation.
Glenohumeral relationship
The head should sit against the glenoid; an empty glenoid = dislocation.
Proximal humerus
Head, tubercles and surgical neck — check the cortical outline for fracture lines.
R Recall checklist — bones
  • Clavicle — S-shaped strut; sternal end (triangular) → SC joint, acromial end (flat) → AC joint; middle/lateral-third junction fractures easily.
  • Clavicle inferior surface — coracoclavicular (conoid tubercle + trapezoid line), costoclavicular, subclavius.
  • Scapula — 2 surfaces, 2 angles, 3 borders, 3 processes (coracoid, acromion, spine); glenoid + labrum; supra/infraglenoid tubercles = biceps/triceps long heads.
  • Fossae — supraspinous, infraspinous, subscapular = the three cuff-muscle beds (+ subscapularis).
  • Proximal humerus — head, anatomical neck, greater/lesser tubercles, bicipital groove ('lady between 2 majors'), surgical neck (axillary nerve!), deltoid tuberosity.
§2Joints · LO3

Joints of the shoulder region

Three joints; for each: surfaces, ligaments, class, movements.

The shoulder region has three synovial joints — sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular and glenohumeral. Describe each the same way: articular surfaces → ligaments (and the muscles that support it) → structural class → movements.

§2.1Sternoclavicular (SC) joint

  • Surfaces: sternal end of the clavicle + the clavicular notch of the manubrium + a small part of the first costal cartilage. An articular disc divides the cavity into two compartments.
  • Ligaments (capsular thickenings): anterior & posterior sternoclavicular, interclavicular, and costoclavicular.
  • Class: synovial saddle joint that functions as a ball-and-socket.
  • Movements: anteroposterior, vertical (elevation/depression), and some rotation — it is the pivot for all girdle movement.
Label Key — Sternoclavicular joint
Sternal clavicle + manubrium + 1st costal cartilage
The three articulating surfaces of the SC joint.
Articular disc
Splits the cavity into two compartments and bonds to all the ligaments — the key to the joint's strength.
Anterior/posterior SC + interclavicular ligaments
Capsular thickenings resisting displacement.
Costoclavicular ligament
Anchors the clavicle to rib 1 — the main check on elevation.
Clinical · a paradox — clavicle fractures common, SC dislocations rare

The disc is fixed to all the SC ligaments, making the joint extremely strong. So force travelling along the clavicle blows the bone before it dislocates the joint — the reason clavicle fractures are common while SC dislocation is rare (and, when posterior, dangerous because the trachea/great vessels sit right behind).

§2.2Acromioclavicular (AC) joint

  • Surfaces: small facets on the acromial end of the clavicle and the acromion, covered by fibrocartilage.
  • Ligaments: the capsule is reinforced by the superior acromioclavicular ligament; true stability comes from the extrinsic coracoclavicular ligament (its trapezoid and conoid bands), which slings the scapula from the clavicle and bears the limb's weight.
  • Class: synovial plane joint. Movements: gliding, letting the scapula rotate on the clavicle.
Label Key — Acromioclavicular joint
AC joint + superior AC ligament
Small plane joint; the superior ligament reinforces the capsule.
Coracoclavicular ligament
The strong extrinsic sling from coracoid to clavicle — the weight-bearing stabiliser.
Trapezoid band
Lateral band → trapezoid line of the clavicle.
Conoid band
Medial band → conoid tubercle of the clavicle.
Clinical · AC separation and the 'step' deformity

A fall onto the point of the shoulder sprains/tears the AC and (in higher grades) the coracoclavicular ligaments. The scapula/limb drop under gravity while the clavicle stays up, so the lateral clavicle rides above the acromion — a palpable, visible step deformity (Plate 2.3). Grading depends on whether the coracoclavicular ligament is intact.

Label Key — AC separation
Step deformity
The lateral clavicle sits proud of the dropped acromion — the classic AC-separation sign.
Mechanism
Direct blow to the shoulder tip; severity tracks with coracoclavicular ligament damage.

§2.3Glenohumeral (shoulder) joint

  • Surfaces: the glenoid cavity (deepened by the labrum) + the head of the humerus.
  • Class: a true ball-and-socket synovial joint — the most mobile joint in the body.
  • Trade-off: great range of movement, weak stability — mobility is bought at the cost of security.
Label Key — Glenohumeral joint
Glenoid cavity + labrum
Shallow socket deepened by a fibrocartilage rim; still takes only ~1/3 of the head.
Head of humerus
Large ball — the mismatch with the small socket is what allows huge range.
Joint capsule
Lax and roomy (especially inferiorly) to permit movement — a weak point for dislocation.

Ligaments — intrinsic and extrinsic

  • Intrinsic (capsular thickenings): coracohumeral ligament; glenohumeral ligaments (superior, middle, inferior bands, anteriorly); and the transverse humeral ligament, which bridges the tubercles to keep the long head of biceps in its groove.
  • Extrinsic: the coracoacromial ligament — with the acromion and coracoid it forms the coraco-acromial (osseoligamentous) arch over the humeral head.
Label Key — Glenohumeral ligaments
Coracohumeral ligament
Coracoid → greater tubercle; supports the superior capsule.
Glenohumeral ligaments (sup/mid/inf)
Anterior capsular reinforcements; the inferior band is the key check in abduction/external rotation.
Transverse humeral ligament
Roofs the bicipital groove, holding the long head of biceps tendon in place.
Label Key — Coraco-acromial arch
Coracoacromial ligament
Spans coracoid to acromion — the roof of the arch.
Acromion + coracoid process
The bony pillars; together with the ligament they overlie the head.
Function
Prevents superior displacement of the head — but the supraspinatus tendon + subacromial bursa are squeezed under it (impingement).
Reasoning · why the arch protects and yet causes impingement

The coraco-acromial arch is a ceiling that stops the humeral head (and the pull of deltoid) from riding upward out of the joint. But the supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa must pass through the narrow space beneath it. Anything that narrows that space — a bone spur, a swollen bursa, a weak cuff letting the head drift up — pinches those structures: subacromial impingement.

Clinical · shoulder dislocation — anterior-inferior and 'pointed shoulder'

Because the capsule is weakest antero-inferiorly (no muscle/tendon reinforcing it there) and the arch blocks superior escape, the head almost always dislocates anteriorly/inferiorly — typically from abduction + external rotation. The rounded deltoid contour is lost, leaving a squared-off 'pointed shoulder' (Plate 2.7). Watch the axillary nerve (§1.3) — commonly injured.

Label Key — Shoulder dislocation
Pointed / squared shoulder
The dislocated head leaves the deltoid contour flattened — a visible sign.
Antero-inferior displacement
The commonest direction, given the weak inferior capsule and the blocking arch above.
Axillary nerve at risk
Assess deltoid power + 'regimental badge' sensation after any dislocation.

Scapulohumeral rhythm

Full arm elevation is not the glenohumeral joint alone — the scapula rotates too (Plate 2.8). Overall abduction is roughly 2:1 — about 2° at the glenohumeral joint for every 1° of scapular rotation (≈120° GH + ≈60° scapular for ~180° total).

Label Key — Scapulohumeral rhythm
Glenohumeral component
~120 degrees of the total arc — the humerus on the glenoid.
Scapular rotation
~60 degrees — the scapula swings its glenoid upward (trapezius + serratus anterior).
~2:1 ratio
Keeps the glenoid under the head throughout the range, preserving stability while reaching overhead.
Reasoning · why the scapula must rotate too

If the humerus alone tried to reach overhead, the head would run out of glenoid and the deltoid would lose its pulling angle. By rotating the scapula (trapezius up top + serratus anterior below form a force couple), the glenoid stays tucked under the moving head — maintaining contact and keeping deltoid effective. Lose serratus (long thoracic nerve palsy, §3.1) and overhead reach fails + the scapula wings.

R Recall checklist — joints
  • SC joint — clavicle + manubrium + 1st costal cartilage; articular disc (2 compartments); saddle acting as ball-and-socket; very strong (disc binds all ligaments).
  • AC joint — acromion + acromial clavicle; plane/gliding; stabilised by the extrinsic coracoclavicular ligament (trapezoid + conoid); injury → step deformity.
  • GH joint — glenoid + labrum + humeral head; ball-and-socket; max mobility, weak stability.
  • GH ligaments — intrinsic: coracohumeral, glenohumeral (sup/mid/inf), transverse humeral; extrinsic: coracoacromial (arch).
  • Dislocation — antero-inferior, 'pointed shoulder', axillary-nerve risk; scapulohumeral rhythm ≈ 2:1 (GH:scapular).
§3Muscles · LO4

Muscles of the shoulder region

Extrinsic movers of the girdle + intrinsic movers/stabilisers of the joint.

Split the muscles into extrinsic (thoracoappendicular — trunk to girdle) and intrinsic (scapula/clavicle to humerus):

  • Extrinsic — anterior: pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, subclavius, serratus anterior.
  • Extrinsic — posterior superficial: trapezius, latissimus dorsi.
  • Extrinsic — posterior deep: levator scapulae, rhomboid minor, rhomboid major.
  • Intrinsic: deltoid, teres major, and the rotator cuff (SITS) — supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.

§3.1Extrinsic — anterior group

Label Key — Anterior group
Pectoralis major
Broad fan from clavicle + sternum/costal cartilages to the lateral lip of the bicipital groove.
Pectoralis minor
Deep to pec major; ribs 3-5 → coracoid process.
Subclavius
Small strut under the clavicle.
Serratus anterior
Wraps the chest wall from ribs 1-8 to the medial scapular border.
  • Pectoralis major — two heads (clavicular + sternocostal) → lateral lip of the bicipital groove. Nerve: lateral & medial pectoral nerves. Action: adduction + medial rotation; clavicular head flexes the humerus, sternocostal head extends it from a flexed position. (Plate 3.2.)
  • Pectoralis minor — ribs 3-5 → coracoid process. Nerve: medial pectoral. Action: stabilises/protracts + depresses the scapula; accessory muscle of respiration when the girdle is fixed.
  • Subclavius — anchors and depresses the clavicle, cushioning the SC joint.
  • Serratus anterior — the "boxer's muscle" (L. serratus = saw) — ribs 1-8 → costal surface of the medial scapular border. Nerve: long thoracic nerve. Action: protracts the scapula and holds it to the chest wall (punching/reaching), and rotates it for overhead reach. (Plate 3.3.)
Label Key — Pectoralis major
Clavicular head
Flexes the humerus (and assists deltoid's anterior fibres).
Sternocostal head
Adducts + medially rotates; extends the flexed humerus back down.
Insertion — lateral lip of bicipital groove
The 'major' on the lateral lip (see the 'lady between two majors').
Label Key — Serratus anterior
Ribs 1-8 origin
The saw-toothed origin along the lateral chest wall.
Medial scapular border (costal) insertion
Pulls the scapula forward against the ribs (protraction).
Long thoracic nerve
Its sole supply — vulnerable, and its loss causes winging.
Clinical · winged scapula (long thoracic nerve / serratus anterior)

Serratus anterior is supplied only by the long thoracic nerve, which runs superficially down the chest wall (vulnerable in surgery/trauma). Paralysis stops the scapula being held to the ribs, so it lifts off — a winged scapula, most obvious when pushing against a wall — and overhead abduction fails (no upward scapular rotation).

§3.2Extrinsic — posterior superficial group

  • Trapezius — origin: superior nuchal line, nuchal ligament, spinous processes C7-T12; insertion: lateral 1/3 clavicle, acromion, scapular spine. Action by region: superior fibres elevate, middle fibres retract, inferior fibres depress the scapula. Nerve: spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) motor + C3/C4 sensory. (Plate 3.4.)
  • Latissimus dorsi — the broadest back muscle; origin: spinous processes T7-T12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, lower 4 ribs; insertion: floor of the bicipital groove. Action: extension, adduction, medial rotation of the humerus; raises the body to the arms in climbing. Nerve: thoracodorsal nerve. (Plate 3.5.)
Label Key — Trapezius
Superior fibres
Elevate the scapula (shrug); with serratus, rotate the glenoid up.
Middle fibres
Retract (adduct) the scapula.
Inferior fibres
Depress the scapula; also part of the upward-rotation force couple.
Accessory nerve (CN XI)
Motor supply — tested by shrug; C3/C4 carry sensation.
Label Key — Latissimus dorsi
Broad origin
T7-T12 spines, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, lower ribs.
Insertion — floor of bicipital groove
The 'LADY' (Latissimus) in the floor of the groove.
Action
Extends, adducts, medially rotates the arm; pulls the body up in climbing.
Thoracodorsal nerve
Its supply.

§3.3Extrinsic — posterior deep group

  • Levator scapulae — transverse processes C1-C4 → superior medial scapular border; elevates the scapula and tilts the glenoid inferiorly (downward rotation).
  • Rhomboid minor & major — retract the scapula and also rotate it to tilt the glenoid inferiorly.
  • All three are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve.
Label Key — Levator scapulae & rhomboids
Levator scapulae (C1-C4 TPs)
Elevates the scapula; downward-rotates the glenoid.
Rhomboid minor / major
Retract the scapula toward the spine; downward-rotate the glenoid.
Dorsal scapular nerve
Common supply to all three.

§3.4Intrinsic — deltoid & teres major

  • Deltoid — the multipennate cap giving the shoulder its rounded contour (inverted Δ); origin: lateral 1/3 clavicle, acromion, scapular spine; insertion: deltoid tuberosity. Actions: anterior fibres flex, middle fibres abduct (after the first 15°), posterior fibres extend. Nerve: axillary nerve. (Plate 3.7.)
  • Teres major — inferior lateral scapular border → medial lip of the bicipital groove; adduction + medial rotation. Nerve: lower subscapular nerve. (Plate 3.8.)
Label Key — Deltoid
Anterior fibres
Flex the arm (with pec major clavicular head).
Middle fibres
Chief abductor — but only after supraspinatus starts the first 15 degrees.
Posterior fibres
Extend the arm (with latissimus dorsi).
Axillary nerve
Supply — paralysed in surgical-neck fracture/dislocation → no abduction.
Label Key — Teres major
Origin — inferior lateral scapular border
Runs up to the humerus with latissimus dorsi.
Insertion — medial lip of bicipital groove
The other 'major' flanking the 'lady' (latissimus).
Action
Adducts + medially rotates the arm (a latissimus helper).
Lower subscapular nerve
Its supply.
Reasoning · why supraspinatus starts abduction and deltoid finishes it

At 0 degrees the deltoid's pull is almost vertical along the humerus — it would just jam the head up into the arch, not swing the arm out. Supraspinatus pulls more horizontally and both initiates the first ~15 degrees and pulls the head into the glenoid, giving deltoid a working angle. From ~15 degrees the deltoid's middle fibres take over as prime abductor. It is a hand-off, not a competition.

§3.5The rotator cuff (SITS)

Four scapulohumeral muscles form a musculotendinous sheath that hugs the humeral head — the shoulder's dynamic stabilisers (Plate 3.9):

  • Supraspinatus (supraspinous fossa → greater tubercle) — abducts 0-15°, initiates abduction, assists deltoid.
  • Infraspinatus (infraspinous fossa → greater tubercle) — lateral (external) rotation.
  • Teres minor (upper lateral scapular border → greater tubercle) — lateral rotation.
  • Subscapularis (subscapular fossa → lesser tubercle) — medial (internal) rotation + adduction (Plate 3.10).
Label Key — Rotator cuff (SITS)
Supraspinatus
Above the spine → greater tubercle; initiates abduction (first 15 degrees).
Infraspinatus
Below the spine → greater tubercle; lateral rotator.
Teres minor
Lateral border → greater tubercle; lateral rotator.
Subscapularis
Costal surface → lesser tubercle; medial rotator — the only anterior cuff muscle.
Label Key — Subscapularis & spaces
Subscapularis (subscapular fossa → lesser tubercle)
Medial rotator + adductor; forms the anterior wall of the axilla.
Quadrangular space
Transmits the axillary nerve + posterior circumflex humeral vessels.
Teres major / latissimus
Borders of the triangular/quadrangular spaces around the scapula.

Nerve supply of the cuff: subscapularis — upper & lower subscapular nerves; supraspinatus & infraspinatus — suprascapular nerve; teres minor — axillary nerve.

Reasoning · why the cuff is a 'dynamic' stabiliser

The bony socket is too shallow to hold the head, and the ligaments only tighten at the extremes of movement. Through the mid-range, stability comes from the four cuff tendons actively pulling the head into the glenoid as the big movers (deltoid, pecs, lats) yank on the arm — a live, tension-adjusting grip. That is why 'strengthen the rotator cuff' is the answer to so much shoulder instability.

Clinical · rotator cuff tears & impingement — supraspinatus first

Supraspinatus is the cuff's weak link: its tendon runs through the tight subacromial space under the coraco-acromial arch (§2.3), so it is the one that impinges and tears. Signs: a painful arc of abduction (~60-120 degrees), weak initiation of abduction, and a positive 'empty can' test. Chronic impingement also inflames the subacromial bursa (§3.6).

Memory hook · SITS + where they insert

SITS = Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis. The first three (S,I,T) insert on the greater tubercle; only Subscapularis (the anterior one) hits the lesser tubercle.

§3.6Bursae of the shoulder

Bursae are fluid-filled sacs that cut friction where tendons rub on bone/ligament or where skin moves over a bony point (Plate 3.11). Around the shoulder:

  • Subtendinous bursa of subscapularis — between the subscapularis tendon and the neck of the scapula (communicates with the joint).
  • Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursa — between the deltoid/acromion above and the supraspinatus tendon/capsule below; lets the cuff glide under the arch.
Label Key — Shoulder bursae
Subacromial / subdeltoid bursa
Cushions the supraspinatus tendon under the acromion + deltoid; inflamed in impingement.
Subscapularis bursa
Between subscapularis and the scapular neck; often continuous with the joint cavity.
Function
Reduce friction where the cuff tendons glide against bone and the arch.
Clinical · subacromial bursitis

The subacromial bursa sits in the impingement zone, so it inflames alongside supraspinatus problems — subacromial bursitis gives a painful arc and tenderness under the acromion. It's why cuff impingement, bursitis and supraspinatus tendinopathy so often travel together.

R Recall checklist — muscles
  • Extrinsic anterior — pec major (adduct/medial rotate; lateral lip groove), pec minor (ribs 3-5 → coracoid), subclavius, serratus anterior (long thoracic n. → winged scapula).
  • Extrinsic posterior — trapezius (CN XI; elevate/retract/depress), latissimus dorsi (thoracodorsal; floor of groove), levator scapulae + rhomboids (dorsal scapular n.; retract/downward-rotate).
  • Intrinsic — deltoid (axillary n.; flex/abduct/extend by part), teres major (lower subscapular n.; medial lip groove).
  • Abduction hand-off — supraspinatus 0-15°, then deltoid middle fibres.
  • Rotator cuff SITS — S/I/T → greater tubercle; Subscapularis → lesser tubercle; dynamic stabilisers; supraspinatus tears/impinges first.
  • Cuff nerves — subscapular (subscapularis), suprascapular (supra + infraspinatus), axillary (teres minor).
  • Bursae — subacromial/subdeltoid (impingement/bursitis) + subscapularis.
